articles.title: In 1976, a Texas Czech festival began as a fundraiser; 50 years later, couples married that year returned to its parade as grandparents with their children and grandchildren
articles.summary: US News: In the small city of West, Texas, a annual celebration of Czech heritage began in 1976 as a modest fundraiser to support the local community. What sta.
articles.body: In the small city of West, Texas, a annual celebration of Czech heritage began in 1976 as a modest fundraiser to support the local community. What started as a single day of polka music, kolaches and a hometown parade has grown over five decades into one of the state’s most beloved cultural festivals. In 2026, the year of Westfest’s 50th anniversary, couples who had been married during the first year of the festival returned to march in the parade, now as grandparents, surrounded by their children and grandchildren. As KWBU reported , the milestone highlighted how a community event rooted in immigrant traditions can become a multigenerational touchstone, uniting families and neighbors over the span of half a century. A small town with deep Czech roots West, Texas, is located on Interstate 35 between Dallas and Austin, a place where the smell of baking kolaches often welcomes visitors before they even cross the town limits . The area was settled in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Czech and Slovak immigrants who arrived in search of land and opportunity .They brought with them their language, Catholic faith, folk music, dance and recipes that would become defining features of the community.For generations, Czech identity in West was lived in everyday ways. Families spoke Czech at home, attended mass at the local Catholic church, and gathered for weddings, funerals and holidays that followed old country customs. Over time, English became dominant and younger generations drifted toward broader American culture, but the markers of Czech heritage remained strong, especially in food, music and community celebrations.The birth of a festivalIn the mid 1970s, community leaders in West were looking for ways to raise funds for local projects and to strengthen civic pride. They decided to organise a festival that would celebrate the town’s Czech roots while drawing visitors from across the region. The first Westfest was held in 1976, featuring a parade, live polka bands, traditional dance groups, food booths and a queen pageant. Kolaches, klobasy and other Czech inspired foods were front and centre, offering a taste of the town’s culinary heritage.The event was an immediate success. Residents turned out in force, and visitors from nearby towns and cities came to experience the music, food and small town atmosphere. What began as a fundraiser quickly became an annual tradition, with each year building on the last. The parade grew longer, the crowds larger and the programming more elaborate, but the core focus on Czech culture and community remained unchanged.Fifty years of music, food and traditionOver five decades, Westfest has become a fixture on the Texas cultural calendar. The festival now spans multiple days, with events that include a grand parade, royalty coronation, carnival rides, craft vendors, 5K runs and continuous performances of Czech and polka music. Dance troupes in folk costumes perform traditional routines, passing down steps and songs that were once common in village squares in Bohemia and Moravia.Food remains a central draw. Local bakeries and vendors sell thousands of kolaches, fruit filled pastries that have become synonymous with Czech Texas. Savory klobasy, roast chicken and other specialties are prepared in large quantities, often using recipes that have been in families for generations. For many attendees, the taste of a fresh kolach is inseparable from the memory of past festivals, family gatherings and childhood visits to West.The parade is the emotional heart of the celebration. Local schools, church groups, civic organisations and businesses march alongside classic cars, fire trucks and floats that reflect both Czech themes and contemporary community life. Grand marshals are often chosen for their long service to the town or their connection to the festival’s history. Over the years, the parade has documented the changing face of West, from agricultural roots to a more diversified economy, while maintaining a strong sense of continuity.A homecoming for the class of 1976The 50th anniversary of Westfest in 2026 offered a natural moment for reflection. Organisers reached out to residents who had been part of the first festival, including couples who were married in or around 1976. Many of these couples had attended Westfest throughout their lives, first as young adults, then as parents bringing their own children to the parade and dances.For the golden anniversary, several of these couples returned to march in the parade as grandparents, accompanied by their children and grandchildren. Some wore sashes or carried signs noting their 50 years of participation. Others just walked together, pointing out landmarks along the route and telling stories of how the festival had changed and remained the same. For them, Westfest was not just an event but a timeline of their lives, marking milestones like marriages, births, graduations and losses. Seeing multiple generations walk side by side in the parade made the passage of time visible in a way that few other local traditions do. Teenagers who had once ridden on floats now pushed strollers. Former festival queens watched their own granddaughters compete in the pageant. The continuity was both personal and communal, a reminder that the festival’s endurance depends on families choosing to return year after year.Keeping heritage alive in a changing worldWestfest’s survival is genuinely impressive at a time when small-town festivals everywhere are folding. Between shifting demographics, digital distractions, and volunteer burnout, keeping an annual tradition alive is tough work. West also had to endure far deeper trauma after the tragic 2013 fertilizer plant explosion that devastated the community and killed fifteen residents.Yet the festival survived by striking a smart balance between tradition and fresh energy. Organizers modernized the event by bringing in bigger carnival rides, diverse live music, and active social media marketing to draw in younger families. At the same time, they kept the heart of the festival untouched, continuing the solemn memorial mass, authentic Czech folk dancing, and beloved homemade recipes.Beyond the local economic boost, Westfest keeps a unique heritage alive for the next generation. Kids grow up learning traditional dances, catching snippets of the Czech language in songs, and connecting specific foods with family celebrations. Even if they never become fluent, they walk away with a deep sense of identity and pride in where they come from.More than a celebrationFor many in West and the surrounding region, Westfest is more than a weekend of events. It is a reunion, a homecoming and a reaffirmation of community ties. People who have moved away often plan their year around the festival, returning to reconnect with relatives, friends and neighbours. Local businesses count on the influx of visitors, and civic groups use the occasion to fundraise and recruit volunteers.The 50th anniversary underscored how deeply the festival is woven into the fabric of local life.When couples who were married in 1976 walked the parade route with their descendants, they were not just celebrating a milestone. They were embodying the festival’s original purpose, to bring people together around shared heritage and shared place. In doing so, they offered a vision of what Westfest might look like at 75 or 100 years, with new generations taking up the same roles their grandparents once held.Looking to the next 50 yearsAs the 2026 celebration concluded, organisers and residents alike looked ahead. The challenge will be to keep Westfest vibrant and relevant while preserving the traditions that make it unique. That will mean continuing to welcome new families, supporting local Czech culture and finding ways to honour the past without being trapped by it.If the first 50 years are any guide, the festival has a strong foundation. It began as a fundraiser and became a institution. It survived disasters and demographic shifts. It grew from a single day into a multi day event that draws tens of thousands of visitors. Most importantly, it remained a place where families could see their own stories reflected in the parade, the music and the shared meal of a warm kolach on a Texas autumn day.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Police launch AI Bobbi chatbot to cut down on non-emergency calls
articles.summary: Merseyside Police are the first police force in the North West to roll-out an AI-powered chatbot.
articles.body:
A North West police force has launched a new "AI-powered virtual police assistant" on its website in a bid to cut down on non-emergency calls.

Merseyside Police has introduced Bobbi, a chatbot the force said is to be used by the public for non-emergency police-related queries.

The virtual assistant can give guidance and connect users to the right services, the force said.

"We are the first force in the North West to roll this out," Supt Tony Fairhurst told BBC Radio Merseyside . "20% of the calls we get to Merseyside Police don't need to be dealt with by a policing operator. AI Bobbi will deal with non-urgent matters - and therefore free up the time for officers."

Supt Fairhurst explained that AI Bobbi is not a replacement for genuine emergency 999 calls - but an alternative for non-emergency scenarios.

"It doesn't replace anything," Fairhurst said of the new tool.

"When anyone rings 999, it doesn't interfere with the emergency process.

"But we get around 2,000 calls a day to Merseyside Police and we know that 20% of these calls don't need a policing operator to deal with them.

"But now someone can go on the website, interact with the chatbot and it will deal with non-urgent matters."

Fairhurst said the process asks the user if their scenario is an emergency - if so, the user is told to call 999.

If not, the user is directed to inputting their name, email address and phone number before describing the problem to the chatbot.

"Then we can deal with it automatically through the chatbot in order to get the right information and the right response to that member of the public," Fairhurst explained.

He maintained the system would not replace existing services like 101 - but would be an additional feature for those comfortable using it.

"101 is not going away," he said. "We're still here and we still have contact resolution officers dealing with those calls every single day.

"This provides an additional service to the public where those that are comfortable using that digital service can get information quicker, faster and also makes sure our contact resolution officers are available for when someone needs to ring 999 that they can be answered immediately."

Asked whether the system poses risks, Fairhurst said the data put into the chatbot is "as safe as any other of our police systems".

He also said inputting information is not mandatory and the chatbot itself will "recognise if a situation escalates" and "ask the person to ring 999."

Similarly, when asked about the bot's ability to recognise signs of mental health distress, Fairhurst said the technology is "trained to understand and interpret how people are feeling".

"It can detect if someone's getting agitated, someone's distressed and it uses all that information then to escalate - where necessary - to a digital operator who can then have that interaction," he said.

He also said the bot will be trained to understand incorrect spelling and grammar - as well as allowing conversations in different languages as well as English.

articles.title: UK economy sees surprise growth in July helped by AI boom
articles.summary: The economy expanded by 0.4%, official figures show, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.
articles.body:
The UK's economy grew faster than expected in July partly helped by businesses using artificial intelligence (AI).

The economy expanded by 0.4%, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, whereas analysts had predicted no growth.

Growth in July was helped by a strong performance from the services sector, and particularly computer programming.

Experts said the figure showed the UK economy was proving resilient in the face of shocks such as the war in Iran, but they expect growth to slow in the months ahead as high energy prices affect households.

July's figure follows growth of 0.3% in June and zero growth in May.

According to the ONS director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, there was evidence that businesses involved with AI and related technologies helped to boost the sector, not just in July but in May and June as well.

The ONS said many of the IT businesses reporting the largest turnover "appear to be involved with AI", though it said it is difficult to quantify the exact impact of AI.

McKeown also said some businesses had said that the warm weather and football world cup had affected activity in July, although she said the effects "differed across industries, benefitting some businesses while creating challenges for others".

The ONS said that in the three months to July, which gives a better underlying picture, the economy grew by 0.4% compared with the previous three months.

Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.

He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.

He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.

Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".

However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.

The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty".

"Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added.

"But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."

Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy , despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures.

"Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you?

Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said while July's headline growth figure was strong, it "masks a weaker picture for households".

"Consumer-facing services contracted in July, as retail and hospitality activity fell following earlier increases in activity in the summer," she said.

"Higher energy and fuel prices are likely to place further pressure on household budgets, while elevated mortgage rates will continue to weigh on housing activity and wider consumer spending."

Richard Carter, the head of fixed interest research at investment firm Quilter Cheviot, said the growth seem in July "may not last, especially as activity is likely to stall ahead of the Budget.

"The war in the Middle East continues to drive a lot of the economic data, but the UK is the most exposed to the fallout," he said.

"Calls for pro-growth measures will get louder as the Budget nears, but whether or not the government has the room to act remains to be seen."

articles.title: Tourist tax likely in Bath and Bristol so visitors 'contribute'
articles.summary: A tourist likely to come into effect, but hospitality leaders fear it could drive customers away.
articles.body:
A new tourist tax for two cities is likely to come into effect, as a council leader says tourists "need to contribute".

Under new government plans, regional mayors will have the power to introduce a tax on overnight accommodation stays in places like Bristol and Bath.

Helen Godwin, mayor of the West of England Combined Authority (Weca), said she was in favour of the scheme, with hopes the money could be reinvested into improving transport. But hospitality leaders fear it could drive off customers.

The leader of Bath and North East Somerset Council, councillor Kevin Guy, said: "There are five million visitors every year to the city of Bath alone, and they have a huge impact on the public realm."

Speaking to BBC Radio Bristol, Guy added: "I've been very clear since the start, those five million visitors need to contribute towards the pavements, the public toilets, the public realm in general, and that will improve things for everybody, tourists and residents."

Pramod Shaw, deputy chair of the Bristol Hoteliers Association, said: "Adding yet another charge risks making Bristol a less attractive proposition compared to other UK cities that may choose not to implement a levy."

He said the industry had "already absorbed significant financial pressures" which had "taken their toll".

Shaw added that talk of the levy had "reignited fury across the business travel and hospitality industries, as this is not the time to add yet another cost to our sectors".

"If a levy is introduced, it must be fair, transparent and must be invested back into the visitor economy," he said.

Caron Cooper, who has owned Fosse Farmhouse bed and breakfast near Castle Combe in Wiltshire, for 42 years, said the tourism industry had been "challenging" in recent years due to the Covid-19 pandemic and increasing business rates.

"Just as we felt like we are coming through it and tourism's back, this is like a hammer blow really," she said.

Cooper added that many people travel around the UK for purposes other than going on holiday, like to visit relatives or see children at university.

"They have a tight budget like everyone else and this is just going to be more that they have to pay out."

"People that are going to five star hotels and spending £500 a night probably won't notice another 5%. But those that are staying at bed and breakfasts and economise then 5% on top of that is going to be a lot," she said.

She added that a flat rate levy would have been a better and more affordable option, in her opinion.

Tourist taxes are used in some European cities, and a similar scheme already exists in Edinburgh.

The levy is likely to be imposed in Bristol, South Gloucestershire and Bath and North East Somerset, which is part of the Weca region.

Godwin said it would help fund further investment there.

"We know that local people want to see further improvements to our transport network, particularly our buses," said Godwin.

"More late-night services would help more people to enjoy what our region has to offer - and so would more funding for public spaces in central Bath and Bristol, as well as support for sectors that support tourism."

Councillor Mike Bell, the leader of North Somerset Council, issued a statement in support of the proposal, but said any funds raised in an area should be invested back into that area.

"Our visitor economy is worth nearly £200m a year, employs a large number of local people and is an important sector to us," he said.

"However, we must also ensure that the extra costs of supporting millions of visitors to our area does not place an undue burden on local finances. Critically, funds from visitors to North Somerset should be invested in North Somerset."

In a joint statement, Guy and the leaders of Bristol City Council and South Gloucestershire Council said the levy was something they had "long campaigned for", but that they would work with local businesses to ensure the funds have positive impacts on local communities.

"We are committed to working closely with businesses across the tourism and hospitality sector to ensure that any future visitor levy is designed in a way that actively supports the industry, help destinations thrive and delivers benefits for local communities," they say.

articles.title: Six houses, Lamborghinis and dozens of Louis Vuitton bags: How a $250 million crypto fraud allegedly funded a luxury life
articles.summary: US News: A $250 million crypto fraud allegedly financed a lavish lifestyle of luxury homes, Lamborghinis, Rolex watches and dozens of Louis Vuitton bags, accor.
articles.body: A $250 million crypto fraud allegedly financed a lavish lifestyle of luxury homes, Lamborghinis, Rolex watches and dozens of Louis Vuitton bags, according to the US Department of Justice. Christopher Alexander Delgado, former CEO of Goliath Ventures, pleaded guilty after admitting that his scheme caused at least $250 million in losses to investors. Prosecutors said investors were promised monthly returns from cryptocurrency “liquidity pools”, but their money was instead used to pay earlier investors, fund lavish travel and buy high-end assets. At least six residential properties were purchased, alongside luxury vehicles, watches and jewellery, as the alleged Ponzi scheme unravelled.Luxury life behind the $250 million crypto fraudAccording to the US Department of Justice, Goliath attracted investors with promises of monthly returns generated through cryptocurrency liquidity pools. The operation used personal referrals, professional marketing materials, luxury events, charitable sponsorships and some monthly payments presented as investment returns to build trust among investors. In reality, prosecutors said, the money was primarily used to return principal to those requesting it and for lavish spending.The scale of the spending was striking. According to the plea agreement and court documents, Delgado used investor funds to acquire at least six residential properties, with each property valued between $1.15 million and $8.5 million. The DOJ also said millions of dollars went to high-end vehicles, watches and jewellery, including Lamborghinis, Rolls-Royces and Rolex watches.Delgado’s luxury purchases included Louis Vuitton bagsThe luxury purchases extended well beyond expensive cars and homes. Prosecutors said Delgado's spending included several dozen Louis Vuitton bags, wallets and pieces of luggage, alongside custom Tiffany jewellery. The collection of luxury goods became part of the assets that Delgado agreed to surrender as part of his guilty plea.The DOJ said Delgado has agreed to forfeit eight properties, 11 vehicles, 30 watches, more than 50 luxury bags and wallets, and 29 pieces of high-end jewellery. Cryptocurrency seized by the United States was included in the forfeiture agreement.How Goliath allegedly used investor moneyThe company presented itself to investors as an opportunity to earn returns from cryptocurrency liquidity pools. But the promised investment activity was not what most of the money went to. Instead, funds were used to pay purported returns to earlier investors and repay principal to investors who wanted their money back, while also funding business events, holidays, luxury travel and personal spending.The arrangement continued from at least January 2023 through January 2026. The DOJ described Goliath as a “Ponzi scheme”, in which purported returns for existing investors are paid using money contributed by newer investors. A companion civil asset forfeiture action identified at least $400 million paid by investors to Goliath, while Delgado admitted in his plea agreement that the scheme caused a minimum of $250 million in investor losses.Delgado pleads guilty to three federal chargesUS Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe said the spending was directly tied to the alleged fraud. “Delgado provided fraudulent information to solicit investor funds and then spent his ill-gotten gains on his extravagant lifestyle,” Kehoe stated. He added that his office would continue working with law enforcement partners to investigate fraud schemes and locate and seize assets linked to Delgado's scheme.Delgado pleaded guilty to three federal offences and faces a maximum of 20 years in prison for each fraud count and up to 10 years for the money laundering count. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for 8 October 2026. The case was investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations, while the asset forfeiture proceedings are being handled separately.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
articles.summary: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.
articles.body:
At the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda.

Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years.

At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months.

First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs.

Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader.

Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October.

And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November.

As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government.

Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change?

That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham.

Going by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past.

In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years".

That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's.

Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey.

In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday , Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing.

In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".

It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues.

Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric.

Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?"

Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves.

And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality.

There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary.

In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank , Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation."

On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago.

The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government.

It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine.

"There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'."

That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting.

According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words."

Perhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge.

The new attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has pared back rules introduced under Sir Keir which some ministers believed forced them to be over-cautious about legal risk, thereby slowing down or blocking new policies altogether.

Louise Haigh , Burnham's deputy, has vowed to "strip out needless bureaucracy" from government more generally, citing an example of there being three public consultations between 2019 and 2023 on whether to microchip cats.

"If we can't microchip cats without getting tied up in red tape, it should come as no surprise the public is losing faith that governments can get things done," she said.

As Burnham moves into the next phase of his autumn, there is a recognition from some around him that he will need to produce some more significant policies to underpin his rhetoric.

Those in government familiar with early work on fleshing out his commitment to "public control" of essential services insist the direction of travel is truly radical.

Haigh is responsible for this, chairing a taskforce on how to reverse "over-privatisation" specifically of housing, water, energy and transport.

Burnham may offer more details on these policies at Labour's conference, while he is likely to wait until after then to show his hand on whether he wants continuity or change when it comes to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's reforms to the legal immigration system - a much more divisive issue among Labour MPs.

And whatever their differences on policy, Labour MPs are united on one thing. The fundamental reason they installed a new prime minister was because many of them believed that continuing on the same path meant losing the next general election.

For them, a long-term improvement in Labour's poll ratings would be the most important change of them all.

articles.title: Son appears in court charged with murdering parents in Blackburn
articles.summary: Yasin Leli, 46, is charged with two counts of murder after his parents, 80 and 78, were found stabbed.
articles.body:
A man has appeared in court charged with murdering his parents in their own home.

Ismail Ahmed Yeli, 80, and 78-year-old Fatma Leli were found stabbed to death in a house on Hardman Street in Blackburn on Monday, Lancashire Police said.

Their family described the couple as "inseparable", adding they were "heartbroken" to have lost "the oldest and most cherished members of our family".

Yasin Leli, 46, also of Hardman Street, has been charged with two counts of murder and appeared at Blackburn Magistrates Court where he was told he would next appear at Preston Crown Court on 15 September.

Officers were called to the house at just after 08:20 BST and found the couple had died from multiple stab wounds.

Lancashire Police said: "Our thoughts remain with their loved ones at this distressing time."

The family thanked police for their "professionalism and compassion", as well as local councillors and the wider community and Masjid-e-Quwwatul mosque for their support.

articles.title: In 2018, Burberry disclosed destroying £28.6 million of unsold clothing, perfume and accessories; the company said the practice helped protect brand exclusivity
articles.summary: US News: In 2018, Burberry faced backlash after revealing it destroyed £28.6 million worth of unsold clothing and accessories to maintain brand exclusivity. This controversial practice led to stronger calls for sustainability in the fashion industry and a reversal of their policy.
articles.body: In 2018, Burberry disclosed in its annual report that it had physically destroyed £28.6 million worth of unsold clothing, perfume, and accessories over the previous financial year, a routine practice in luxury retail that became a public controversy as soon as the figure came to light. The disclosure, buried in a lengthy annual filing, drew immediate scrutiny from the media, shareholders and lawmakers, and the company announced in September 2018 that it would stop destroying unsold merchandise except as a last resort.The £28.6 million figure covered the year ending March 31, 2018Burberry's annual report stated that the cost of finished goods physically destroyed that year came to £28.6 million, a figure later cited directly in a UK House of Commons Environmental Audit Committee report examining sustainability across the fashion industry. This was an increase from £26.9 million in the previous year, according to Burberry’s 2017/18 annual report. Among the products destroyed were clothes, accessories and perfume that had not been sold through regular distribution channels. The company chose to burn off the products instead of selling them at a reduced price or donating them away. This, as stated by the company, helped them capture the energy that was released during the process.The company said the goal was protecting brand exclusivity, not simply managing wasteAccording to Burberry, the new policy was designed to prevent any surplus from entering the grey market. The grey market is characterized by discount items that may erode a brand’s premium positioning. By selling the surplus goods at a discount, Burberry said that it could diminish the value of its brand as well as create an opportunity for counterfeiters, because counterfeit products may benefit from discounted goods for legitimacy. The justification provided by Burberry was not uncommon within the fashion retail industry. The committee noted that the Burberry stock-burning case had drawn attention to wider concerns about how fashion companies handled unsold goods.Shareholder and lawmaker scrutiny followed almost immediatelyThe Fixing Fashion report said that “the fashion industry has marked its own homework for too long” and called for stronger government action, including mandatory due diligence and measures to make retailers take greater responsibility for textile waste. The Fixing Fashion report itself cites data showing only 55% of the 150 brands and retailers surveyed by Fashion Revolution's 2018 Transparency Index were publishing measurable, time-bound environmental goals, with just 6% offering repair services. Advocacy groups added to the pressure. The parliamentary committee's findings highlighted the wider problem of unsold stock and called for stronger government action on textile waste.Burberry reversed the policy by September 2018As per a statement issued by Burberry in September 2018, the company stated that in future, Burberry will stop the practice of destroying unsold merchandise and will opt for reusing, repairing, donating, or recycling unsold products as far as possible, destroying them only as a last resort when products are defective, damaged, or obsolete, a carve-out critics noted could still cover much of the unsold seasonal stock the original practice was meant to address. However, legislators in the committee report acknowledged the commitment but claimed that other firms in the industry had failed to do so. In that same September 2018 statement, Burberry separately announced, as an unrelated policy shift, that it would stop using real fur in its products.A recommendation made by the Environmental Audit Committee in their Fixing Fashion report of February 2019 suggested that the British government should stop the practice of burning and burying unsold stocks of clothes that can be recycled and reused. The recommendations did not become laws, but the findings of the committee were largely based on the attention that was garnered by Burberry's disclosure and it was used as an exemplary case where voluntary commitments alone were perceived as insufficient. It was hard to tell whether other British firms were disposing of as many items as Burberry, yet most companies give very little information on the issue as compared to Burberry in their annual reports.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Scotland’s first commercial wind farm recycled and reused 99.9% of materials from 26 old turbines, with blades turned into construction polymers
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Scotland’s first commercial wind farm has reached a major milestone in dealing with turbine waste after almost three decades of operation. Hagshaw Hil.
articles.body: Scotland’s first commercial wind farm has reached a major milestone in dealing with turbine waste after almost three decades of operation. Hagshaw Hill in South Lanarkshire, which began operating in 1995, was decommissioned and repowered with 14 newer turbines after its original 26 turbines were dismantled in 2023. A Mott MacDonald assessment commissioned by ScottishPower Renewables found that 79.5% of materials from the old turbines and associated components were recycled, while another 20.4% were reused, giving a combined recovery rate of 99.9%. The project also found a new use for one of the wind industry's more difficult waste streams, with all the old turbine blades processed by Northern Ireland-based Plaswire into polymer materials for construction and engineering applications.Scotland’s first commercial wind farm gets a new lifeHagshaw Hill began generating electricity in 1995 and became Scotland’s first commercial wind farm. Located in South Lanarkshire, the site operated for almost 30 years before its original turbines were dismantled in 2023 as part of a repowering project. The old installation had 26 turbines, while the replacement project uses 14 much larger and more powerful machines. The Scottish Government approved 14 turbines with a maximum tip height of 200 metres and a maximum generating capacity of 84MW. ScottishPower says the repowered project provides more than 79MW of capacity.99.9% of old materials were recycled or reusedThe Mott MacDonald assessment commissioned by ScottishPower Renewables found that 79.5% of materials from the decommissioned turbines were recycled and 20.4% were reused. Together, the figures represent a 99.9% recycling and reuse rate. Reused components include equipment that has been retained for industry training as the wind sector prepares for more turbine decommissioning and repowering projects.The project also relied heavily on local businesses. ScottishPower says the majority of the recycling and reuse supply chain was located within 30 miles of Hagshaw Hill. At least 10 supply-chain companies in Scotland and elsewhere in the UK received contracts connected with the decommissioning work.Old turbine blades became construction polymersOne of the most notable parts of the project was the treatment of the turbine blades. Unlike metals such as steel, composite blades can be difficult to recycle because they contain layers of materials bonded together. At Hagshaw Hill, all the blades from the original turbines were recycled by Northern Ireland-based Plaswire.The company processed the blade material into its RX Polymer, which can be used in construction and engineering applications. The recycled material can replace products made from virgin plastics, timber and precast concrete. Potential applications include site fencing, marker posts, drainage components and other construction products.Plaswire's process involves processing composite blade material into smaller pieces before incorporating it into the recycled polymer. This gives the old blades a second industrial use instead of sending them for disposal.26 turbines replaced by 14 larger machinesThe Hagshaw Hill repowering project significantly increased the amount of electricity the site can generate. The original 26 turbines had a combined capacity of about 15.6MW. The new development has 14 turbines and more than 79MW of generating capacity, meaning the site's capacity has increased roughly fivefold while the number of turbines has almost halved.ScottishPower says the repowered wind farm can generate enough electricity to power the equivalent of around 57,000 homes. The approved development also includes provision for around 20MW of battery energy storage.The repowering means the established wind-farm site can continue generating renewable electricity with newer, more efficient technology rather than relying on the original turbines installed in the 1990s.A blueprint for future wind-farm repoweringHagshaw Hill's transformation comes as older wind farms around Scotland and the wider UK approach the end of their original operating lives. The project demonstrates how decommissioning and repowering can be combined with large-scale material recovery.ScottishPower says around 1GW of its turbines are expected to come down over the next decade, creating a growing need for recycling and reuse solutions for components such as steel, electrical equipment and composite blades. Hagshaw Hill provides an example of how these materials can be redirected into new uses while newer turbines increase renewable-energy generation.The project has also brought greater benefits to nearby communities. ScottishPower says the repowered wind farm will provide nearly £400,000 a year through its community benefit fund to communities including Coalburn, Douglas, Lesmahagow and Rigside & Douglas Water. The fund is around 26 times larger than the one associated with the original wind farm.Hagshaw Hill has therefore gone from Scotland's first commercial wind farm to an example of how an ageing renewable-energy site can be given a second life, with fewer and more powerful turbines producing substantially more electricity while almost all material from the old installation is recycled or reused.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2023, France expanded funding for a programme to distil nearly 80 million gallons of surplus wine into industrial alcohol; the measure aimed to ease pressure on the market
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2023, France tackled a wine surplus crisis by spending €200 million to distill 80 million gallons of wine into industrial alcohol, addressing reduced consumption and accumulating stocks while reflecting changing consumer preferences for wine.
articles.body: In 2023, France took an unusual initiative to tackle a growing wine surplus challenge. They paid the producers to remove eligible wine from the drinking market and send it to distilleries. This measure was initially designed to cover up to 3 million hectolitres of wine, which is equivalent to about 79 million US gallons. And after a surge in demand, the government ultimately made available as much as €200 million for the crisis-distillation programme. The wine was not simply poured away; instead, it was distilled into alcohol intended for non-food uses, including industrial and energy applications.Following a combination of falling consumption, weaker sales and accumulated stocks faced by producers, particularly in parts of southern France and Bordeaux, the intervention came. The European Commission noted that this crisis reflected reduced consumption, inflation and a good 2022 harvest, contributing to increased wine availability. For producers already holding unsold wine, storage became an issue as the harvest approached, as wineries needed space for incoming production.This pressure was not evenly distributed across the French wine industry. The French crisis-distillation initiative was particularly aimed at certain red and rosé wines, instead of treating every variety and appellation in the country alike.Why France found itself with surplus wineA single bad harvest was not the root of this challenge. French wine consumption had been undergoing a long-term transformation, with red wine losing ground over time. The International Organisation of Vine and Wine reported that French red-wine consumption fell from around 17.8 million hectolitres in 2000 to 9 million hectolitres in 2021. This showed a decline of roughly 49%. Red wine’s share of French wine consumption also declined substantially during this period.Inflation reduced consumers’ purchasing power, and changing post-pandemic consumption patterns also affected wine sales. Concurrently, the European wine market was dealing with substantial supplies, with reports suggesting that the good harvest in 2022 contributed to the accumulation of stocks, while weaker demand left producers with more wine than the market could readily absorb.According to FranceAgriMer, French wine exports in 2023 fell 9% in volume as compared to the exports in 2022, while the export value declined by 3%. The organisation attributed the deterioration in part to economic conditions affecting major markets and noted that stocks accumulated after the pandemic continued to influence trade. This did not mean that France suddenly lost its overseas market. Instead, this indicated that weaker export volumes reduced one of the outlets that could have otherwise helped absorb domestic production.On the other hand, production itself was far from collapsing. French agricultural statistics put the country’s 2023 wine production at roughly 48 million hectolitres, which was above the 2022 level. The growers in affected regions were put in a difficult position with these results. Wine that remained in tanks and cellars represented tied-up capital and occupied storage capacity, while selling large quantities at reduced prices risked putting further downward pressure on the struggling market. Removing some wine from the beverage supply was therefore aimed at addressing the immediate inventory problem rather than simply compensating producers for unsold bottles.The €200 million interventionIn 2023, FranceAgriMer established an initial programme with an €80 million budget. Eligible producers could send qualifying red and rosé wine for distillation, with the resulting alcohol required to be directed toward non-food uses. The rising demand for the programme highlighted that the initial envelope would not be enough. The country’s agriculture ministry reported that applications submitted during the first phase represented more than 4.4 million hectolitres (roughly 116 million US gallons), substantially above the roughly 3 million hectolitres that the programme was initially designed to accommodate. Subsequently, the government increased the resources available for the operation, bringing the maximum budget to €200 million, which successfully expanded the program's capacity to absorb and destroy the 4.4-million-hectolitre (116 million gallons) surge.European Union rules required the resulting alcohol from the process to be kept out of the food-and-drink industry. Depending on the destination, such alcohol could be used for manufacturing or commercial fuel purposes, meaning the programme recovered some material value while ensuring that the excess wine no longer competed with wine producers selling for consumption.The crisis-distillation programme could address an immediate stock problem, but it could not reverse years of changing consumer preferences. Removing millions of litres from the market could reduce the pressure on prices in the short term. However, it would not automatically restore demand for the wine varieties that consumers were buying less frequently.This was why the French government pursued measures aimed at reducing long-term production pressure. They supported vineyard grubbing-up and restructuring measures intended to help growers adapt where existing production was no longer economically viable.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2013, actor Max Thieriot bought a roughly 90-acre Sonoma ranch; more than a decade later, this Hollywood retreat has grown into a working vineyard, farm and family retreat producing its own wine and food
articles.summary: News News: Actor Max Thieriot and his wife Lexi bought a roughly 90-acre ranch in west Sonoma County, California, in 2013, and over the past decade, the property.
articles.body: Actor Max Thieriot and his wife Lexi bought a roughly 90-acre ranch in west Sonoma County, California, in 2013, and over the past decade, the property has evolved into a working vineyard and family retreat. The ranch is located between Bodega and Occidental near where Thieriot grew up.According to Home Archives, three years after buying the ranch, Thieriot and Lexi began planting a vineyard there. About nine acres of the property are now planted with Pinot noir grapes under the name Bodega Thieriot, while the rest of the land remains a mix of hillsides, woodland and pasture.The ranch is also connected to Thieriot’s family history in Sonoma County. He grew up on a separate vineyard property in Occidental that his parents bought in the 1980s. His own ranch is a newer family property, but farming grapes has been part of his life since childhood.Thieriot is now best known as the co-creator and star of the CBS drama Fire Country. However, his connection with Sonoma County has continued through the ranch and vineyard. Although his family now spends most of the year in Washington state, the Sonoma property remains a working vineyard and a place the family returns to during the off-season.The Sonoma ranch and its vineyardThe ranch covers approximately 90 acres of rolling land between Bodega and Occidental. It has mature oak and redwood trees, ocean views and a fence line shared with the Occidental winery of winemaker Steve Kistler.The property is not known for a large celebrity-style residence. Details such as the size of the house, number of bedrooms and interior features have not been publicly reported. The purchase price has also not been disclosed.In 2016, Thieriot and Lexi started planting the vineyard with winemaker Thomas Rivers Brown. Around nine acres of the ranch were planted with Pinot noir, leaving most of the property as hillside, woodland and pasture.The vineyard was named Bodega Thieriot. It is also connected to the family’s earlier winemaking history through Senses Wines, the Sonoma County wine label Thieriot co-founded with Christopher Strieter and Myles Lawrence-Briggs, friends he met in preschool.A second vineyard shaped Thieriot’s childhoodThe Bodega ranch is separate from the vineyard where Thieriot grew up. His parents, Cameron and Bridgit, bought that Occidental property in the 1980s. It has roughly 12 acres planted with Pinot noir and Chardonnay, and its grapes are used by Senses Wines.Thieriot has spoken about growing up around the vineyard and working with his father. “I spent my entire childhood there,” Thieriot has said of the property as quoted by Home Archives. “I have an old photo of me with my dad farming grapes. I grew up riding a tractor with my dad when he farmed in the vineyard.”His mother and sister still live in the area, keeping the family’s connection to west Sonoma County even though Thieriot and his immediate family now live elsewhere for much of the year.How Sonoma influenced Fire CountryThe actor’s connection with the region also influenced his television work. Sonoma County experienced major wildfires in 2017, 2019 and 2020, and Thieriot has said those events helped inspire Fire Country.During the 2017 Tubbs and Nuns fires, he drove back from Los Angeles to help his mother load horse trailers and move livestock from the property.The show is set in Northern California and follows firefighters, while its connection to Thieriot’s home region has remained part of its background. The series is filmed in and around Vancouver, British Columbia, rather than Sonoma County.Thieriot now spends part of the year in SonomaThieriot has said that Fire Country films for roughly nine months of the year. Living closer to the Vancouver-area set reduces the long journey between Washington and Sonoma.The move, however, did not mean leaving the ranch behind. Thieriot continues to return to the Sonoma property when filming is over. “We’re filming nine months of the year, but in the off-season I head back here,” he said.Thieriot has also spoken about wanting his sons to experience the same connection with the land that shaped his own childhood, saying he wants them to grow up “knowing what it’s like to have a vineyard outside their door.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2017, Haiti began replacing kerosene vaccine fridges with 850 solar-powered units; vaccination coverage in the North rose from 73.6% to 86% by the end of 2018
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2017, Haiti transformed its vaccine storage system by replacing outdated kerosene fridges with solar-powered units, leading to a significant increase in vaccination coverage in the North from 73.6% to 86% by 2018, as reported by UNICEF.
articles.body: Health workers once had to rely on refrigerators that were powered by gas or kerosene in northern Haiti, to keep vaccines cold in places where electricity was unreliable. The equipment was expensive to operate and vulnerable to fuel shortages.But a solar-powered cold chain began changing that in 2017, as more than 850 solar refrigerators had been installed across Haiti in less than three years, as reported by UNICEF. In the North, vaccination coverage rose from 73.6% in 2017 to 86% at the end of 2018, according to Derline Mentor, a UNICEF cold-chain officer.A cold chain problem was also a distance problemTransporting fuel to health facilities could be difficult in rural and mountainous parts of Haiti, and a refrigerator could also become useless if its fuel supply was interrupted or if equipment broke and repairs were delayed. UNICEF's account of the program describes the older refrigerators as gas- or kerosene-powered, and health workers said the cost and logistics of maintaining those systems could lead to interruptions in the cold chain.UNICEF said that the solar refrigerators could maintain vaccine temperatures between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius and could be monitored remotely, which allowed health workers to store doses at smaller facilities and then transport them in cool boxes to vaccination sessions in nearby communities.That changed the distance involved in getting a child vaccinated for some families. UNICEF described one mother in the Nord department who previously faced a two- to three-hour journey to the nearest hospital. After a solar refrigerator was installed closer to her community, the vaccination meeting point was about 10 minutes away on foot.Haiti was an early beneficiary of the cold-chain upgradeThe solar refrigerator program was connected to the broader Cold Chain Equipment Optimization Platform supported by Gavi and other partners. Gavi reported that Haiti's health ministry was the first country to use the platform to overhaul its aging vaccine cold chain. In 2017, more than 191 modern solar-powered refrigerators were deployed in rural and mountainous areas.In remote mountain communities, it was difficult carrying propane cylinders to power conventional refrigerators. The new equipment could operate without depending on a regular fuel delivery system. Gavi described the investment as part of a wider push to replace outdated or damaged refrigeration equipment and expand cold-chain capacity in countries where reliable electricity was unavailable.Technicians had to install and maintain the refrigerators, vaccines still had to be transported, and health workers still had to persuade families to attend vaccination sessions. The technology addressed one of the physical barriers in that chain, which was keeping doses within the required temperature range before they reached children.Solar power moved refrigeration closer to patientsUNICEF described nurses taking vaccine doses from a solar refrigerator at a vaccination point in La Suisse, in northern Haiti, and placing them in a cool box and traveling by motorcycle to vaccinate children. The arrangement meant that the refrigerator could support a smaller network of vaccination points.UNICEF later described solar refrigeration as part of its wider effort to strengthen Haiti's immunization cold chain. By 2021, UNICEF said it had installed more than 920 solar-powered refrigerators in Haiti and had equipped 96% of the country's health institutions with solar fridges for vaccine storage.The coverage figure came alongside the equipment rolloutThe increase in northern Haiti's reported vaccination coverage was recorded during the same period in which the solar cold-chain program was expanding. UNICEF reported coverage of 73.6% in the North in 2017 and 86% at the end of 2018. The figures show the change in vaccination coverage, but they do not establish that solar refrigerators alone caused the increase. Other parts of the immunization system were operating at the same time, including vaccine supply, outreach and health-worker services.The refrigerators addressed something more specific, which was the ability to keep vaccines properly stored in places where conventional refrigeration depended on unreliable electricity or fuel. The solar units reduced one of the logistical obstacles between vaccine supply and the children who needed it by bringing cold storage closer to remote communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1998, researchers used fluorescent tracers in Boston’s Fort Point Channel to track polluted sediment; water flushed in 1–2.7 days, but particle removal ran 10 times faster than lab tests
articles.summary: US News: A 1998 study on Boston's Fort Point Channel shows water could be replaced in 1-2.7 days, but suspended particles were removed 10 times faster than lab tests suggested, shedding light on urban water pollution dynamics.
articles.body: A 1998 study of Boston’s Fort Point Channel found that the water in the narrow section of Boston Harbor could be replaced within roughly one to 2.7 days, while suspended particles that carry sediment-like material were removed from the water column at rates about an order of magnitude faster than laboratory settling tests had previously suggested. The researchers were trying to understand what happened to contaminated particles that entered the channel, which is an area that is affected by combined sewer overflows and historically polluted sediment. They released fluorescent tracers and followed their movement through the water rather than relying on observations alone.The study was published in Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science, and used Rhodamine WT as a dissolved tracer to measure water movement. Fluorescent pigment particles were mixed with the dye to represent suspended material with characteristics that could be compared to sewage-associated particles. Water samples were collected across the channel for about a week after each tracer release.The dye and particles did not behave the same wayThis was the central part of the experiment. Rhodamine WT moved with the water and had little interaction with suspended sediment, and researchers could estimate how quickly water itself was being flushed from Fort Point Channel by following changes in its concentration. That produced a replacement time of about 1 to 2.7 days, and the exact rate varied with tidal conditions and freshwater inflow, which meant that the channel did not have one fixed flushing time.The fluorescent particles behaved differently, as their concentration declined relative to the dye, which indicated that some of the suspended material was being removed from the water rather than simply carried out with the moving water. The researchers calculated effective deposition velocities of about 1.5 to 3.3 meters per day, and noted that these values were an order of magnitude faster than rates observed in laboratory settling columns.A layer of material on the bottom may have trapped particlesThe paper proposed that the suspended particles could have been scavenged by a soft bottom layer, and was described by the researchers as a bottom “fluff” layer. The material in that layer could interact with particles that moved through the water and remove them from suspension more quickly than ordinary settling would predict.The observations suggested that interactions at the sediment-water interface were important in determining the fate of suspended material. The result also fit with earlier observations from Salem Sound and with controlled laboratory work on particle aggregation at the sediment-water boundary. Fast disappearance of particles from the water does not necessarily mean that pollution has left the harbor, since a particle that settles onto the bottom may remain within the local environment rather than being transported into the outer harbor.Fort Point Channel was already a difficult place for pollution studiesA Massachusetts Water Resources Authority report on contaminated sediments describes Fort Point Channel as a restricted-flushing area with a major combined sewer overflow at its head. The report said that the channel was important for understanding how dissolved and particle-bound pollutants from combined sewer overflows moved between the inner and outer harbor. Fluorescent tracers were released near the head of the channel and monitored for roughly a week in the earlier tracer surveys. The channel's bridges and geometry also made repeated sampling possible.The same report noted that the largest combined sewer overflow in Boston Harbor was located at the head of the channel at the time of the study. Combined sewer systems can carry both wastewater and stormwater, and overflows can discharge into receiving waters during wet weather. The MWRA now describes CSOs as occasional discharges of rainwater and sewage into Boston Harbor and nearby rivers, although decades of infrastructure work have greatly reduced the volume and frequency of those releases.The study changed the picture of particle transportWater in Fort Point Channel could be replaced within days, but particles could leave the water column much faster than expected from laboratory settling measurements. The researchers attributed the difference, at least in part, to interactions with material that had already accumulated on the channel floor. That meant the fate of contaminants depended not only on how quickly the channel flushed, but also on what happened when suspended particles encountered the sediment at the bottom.A Massachusetts Water Resources Authority study later reported that more than half of contaminated particles entering Fort Point Channel from combined sewer overflows settled and were trapped within the channel rather than reaching the outer harbor.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1998, Minnesota installed 76 automatic de-icer nozzles on an ice-prone Mississippi River bridge; winter crashes later fell from 31 to 10, a 68% reduction
articles.summary: US News: Minnesota's automated de-icing system on the Interstate 35W bridge has dramatically reduced winter accidents by 68%, showcasing the effectiveness of technology in road safety.
articles.body: A bridge deck can freeze solid while the road on either side remains completely clear because, in contrast to an open roadway, cold air moves both above and below it. For many years, the only effective defence was a salt-filled truck that was dispatched anytime circumstances were dangerous and frequently arrived after ice had already formed. After deciding that responding to ice was insufficient, Minnesota's transport experts set out to build a bridge that could heal itself before a single tyre lost traction. The experiment took place on the Interstate 35W bridge in Minneapolis, which crosses the Mississippi River. Due to significant year-round traffic and mist rising from adjacent St. Anthony Falls, the area is prone to black ice. According to Minnesota's Department of Transportation, the state installed its first automated bridge anti-icing system on the old Interstate 35W bridge over the Mississippi River in 1998.Building a bridge that senses its own weatherThe system itself was a Swiss-designed installation supplied by a company called Boschung, and it worked by connecting weather sensors to a network of spray nozzles placed directly into the road surface. The system connected weather sensors to spray nozzles embedded in the bridge deck, while its computer-controlled system could select from 16 different spray patterns depending on storm conditions.Instead of regular salt, the device sprays a chemical called potassium acetate when conditions get hazardous since it works at significantly lower temperatures and is less corrosive to the understructure. Next to the bridge was a tank containing several thousand gallons of the chemical, which could be pumped away automatically the instant sensors detected the possibility of ice forming, without the need for maintenance personnel to be sent out.What the numbers actually showedThe system was subsequently evaluated using operational and crash data, and a federal review reported a 68% reduction in winter-season crashes at the I-35W Mississippi River bridge. The federal evaluation reported a 68% reduction in winter-season crashes at the I-35W Mississippi River bridge, with a benefit-to-cost ratio of 3.4 to 1. The same analysis also found that, depending on the location, automatic anti-icing devices on bridges generally reduced crashes by 25–100%.Ice control becomes commonplaceMinnesota later deployed automated anti-icing systems at other bridges, including sites near Duluth, Winona, and elsewhere in the state. Since then, independent research organisations have compiled a list of several similar projects around the nation, viewing the original Mississippi River bridge as a sort of proof of concept for the entire technology, a case still referenced in transport research archives maintained by the Transportation Research Board. The Minneapolis installation showed that automated bridge anti-icing could reduce winter crashes while treating the road before ice formed. Minnesota subsequently used automated systems at other high-risk bridge locations across the state.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Brics 2026: Trump shadow looms large over Delhi summit as Modi hosts Putin and Xi
articles.summary: As Brics leaders meet in Delhi, divisions within the bloc make a united response to Washington unlikely.
articles.body:
The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend.

Leaders from 11 Brics nations - including host India, China, Russia, Brazil, South Africa, the UAE and Iran, with Saudi Arabia attending as an invited member - will hold talks on a wide range of issues. But few will be as consequential as the impact of President Trump's policies.

The war in Iran and the ever-present threat of White House tariffs, directed at both US adversaries and allies, have destabilised global energy markets and has often left the global economy guessing the future.

It is against this backdrop that Brics leaders are meeting. Yet the group is unlikely to produce a consensus statement that openly calls out the US or lays out a coordinated strategy to counter President Trump's policies and geopolitics.

That is partly because Brics itself is deeply divided over how far it should go in challenging Washington.

"India cannot afford to have a joint statement that rails against Washington," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. He expects any criticism of US policies to be "vague and indirect", reflecting the sharply divergent interests within the expanded group.

While Russia and Iran may push for the group to take a clearer stand against President Trump, the geopolitical realities within Brics are likely to make that difficult.

India, which is reportedly in the final stages of a trade deal with the US, will not want a statement that could upset the White House. China, too, may be wary of being seen as using Brics to target Washington.

Then there is the UAE, which has come under Iranian attack during Tehran's retaliation against US and Israeli strikes. The Gulf state, which hosts US military bases, is unlikely to support a statement that helps Tehran's cause.

Kugelman says Brics has become more significant through its expansion, but that has also made consensus harder.

"You've added a number of members that don't get along," he said, describing the challenge for India as bringing together countries with "a wide array of views and positions on the global order".

Trump has also been quite vocal against Brics, particularly its efforts to reduce global trade's dependence on the US dollar, commonly known as de-dollarisation.

He has often warned the group against trying to come up with an alternative currency or take measures to weaken the dollar's dominance in global trade.

In one such threat, Trump said in November 2024 that Brics countries would face "100% tariffs" if they backed another currency to replace the "mighty US dollar".

Under these circumstances, what can the group realistically deliver?

Brics' geopolitical and economic heft has grown substantially over the past decade. While it will be reluctant to take an openly anti-US or anti-Western position, the group will be looking to build on its existing achievements and demonstrate that it can emerge as an alternative blocs like the G20 and G7.

Brics now accounts for 49% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of international trade, according to BBC Monitoring's analysis.

Its most tangible achievement remains the New Development Bank - which has approved billions of dollars in infrastructure and development projects - many of them in countries of the global south.

The group has also created a $100bn contingency reserve arrangement to help members facing financial crises, although it has yet to be tested.

The leaders are also likely to explore ways to make cross-border payments in local currencies easier. That will be of particular interest to Moscow and Tehran, both of which face severe US sanctions.

Brics is also expected to continue positioning itself as a voice for the developing nations, collectively pushing for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which many developing nations feel do not accurately reflect the new global order.

For India, in particular, the summit offers an opportunity to strengthen its claim to leadership of the global south.

Many of Delhi's own foreign policy priorities, including multilateralism, a more multipolar world, greater representation for developing countries and freer global trade, align closely with Brics' wider agenda.

But India will also have to find ways to work around China's considerable influence within Brics and its stronger presence across much of the developing world.

The Modi government has placed a strong emphasis on becoming a "leader or a voice of the Global South", Kugelman says. But India's efforts have had "limited success" in making deeper inroads in Africa and Latin America, where China has been more successful.

With most Brics members coming from developing economies, Kugelman says the expanded grouping gives India an opportunity to deepen ties with countries such as Ethiopia, Brazil and Indonesia and build a stronger profile across Africa and Latin America.

For Delhi, the test will be whether it can secure a consensus statement - often seen as a measure of a host nation's diplomatic success. That will be difficult given sharp differences over the Iran war, relations with the US and the future of global trade.

The scale of the challenge was evident in May, when Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after their summit because of differences over the Iran war, leaving host India to issue a chair's summary instead.

India will take confidence from its experience as G20 host in 2023, when it managed to secure a joint declaration despite deep divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine.

But Delhi will also want substantive announcements and to highlight what Brics has already achieved. On this, members are likely to agree: none will want the grouping dismissed as merely a "talk shop".

Leaders are expected to explore ways to strengthen financial cooperation and may make substantive announcements. They are also likely to address major geopolitical developments, with any language on the US is expected to be carefully crafted to avoid confrontation.

Washington, for its part, will be watching closely.

The summit will also provide the setting for several important bilateral meetings. Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday will be keenly watched. The two countries have been slowly rebuilding ties, although progress has been more cautious than either side might have hoped.

Modi is also due to meet President Vladimir Putin, with the war in Ukraine likely to feature prominently in their discussions.

Modi made a highly public appeal for peace when he met Putin last month on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek. While some interpreted his remarks as a rebuke to Moscow, Russia did not see them that way and publicly welcomed Modi's efforts.

Beyond geopolitics, India's growing trade deficit with both Russia and China is also likely to feature in the bilateral discussions.

But in the end, the group's focus will be on concluding a successful summit as it would add further weight to Brics' influence.

And for host India, it would also be a diplomatic and geopolitical achievement at a time when Delhi is seeking to reassert its international influence.

Kugelman says the stakes are particularly high for India at this summit.

Delhi, he argues, has been somewhat overshadowed by Pakistan's recent diplomatic role in the Middle East, including its involvement in mediation efforts around the Iran war.

"This is an important opportunity for India to reassert its global significance and its global leadership," he says. "That is one reason why the stakes are high."

The summit, he adds, is in some ways "more important for India as host than it is for the Brics grouping as a whole".
