articles.title: Black Axe in South Africa: Six Nigerians Nigerians accused of romance scams to be extradited to the US
articles.summary: The six will face wire fraud and money-laundry charges in the US, South African police say.
articles.body:
South African police are handing over six Nigerians wanted in the US for alleged online romance scams to FBI agents later on Friday.

The group is accused of targeting over 100 women in the US and defrauding them of more than 100m rand ($6m; £5m), the South African authorities said.

Those being extradited were arrested in 2021 and are believed to be members of crime syndicate Black Axe - a Nigerian mafia-style gang tied to human trafficking, internet fraud and murder.

Some of their reported victims included pensioners and businesspeople "who were targeted through sophisticated online relationships used to defraud them of their money", according to South Africa's elite Hawks police unit.

The group will be "transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town" to the airport on Friday morning, where they will be "handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service", Hawks spokesperson Colonel Katlego Mogale said in a statement.

They would face wire fraud and money-laundering charges upon their arrival in the US, she added.

Mass arrests in global crackdown on West African cyber-crime networks

Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network known for its extreme violence and operates across Africa, Europe and North America.

A BBC Eye investigation in 2021 suggested that the syndicate had become one of the most far-reaching and dangerous organised crime groups in the world.

Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling.

The group has been on the radar of law enforcement agencies for a number of years.

FBI operations against Black Axe were launched in November 2019 and September 2021, eventually charging more than 35 individuals with multi-million dollar internet fraud.

Since then there have been several other operations across multiple countries targeting Black Axe co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol.

Last month, Interpol said during its latest one - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - seven sites in South Africa linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided.

It led to the arrests of 39 people, the seizure of money and the blocking of more than 250 bank accounts.

articles.title: In 2023, a US engineer put a miniature water-treatment plant beneath the sink; the under-$500 unit converted 20% of household greywater into drinking water
articles.summary: US News: Discover the innovative Cycleau, a compact water-treatment system that transforms household greywater into safe drinking water, helping tackle water scarcity challenges.
articles.body: A small space beneath a kitchen or bathroom sink is usually occupied by pipes, cleaning supplies and little else. In 2023, however, young US designer and engineer Noemi Florea was developing a different use for that overlooked space: a compact treatment system capable of treating household greywater to drinking-water quality. According to UNICEF, Noemi Florea developed Cycleau as a compact household water-treatment system designed to fit beneath a sink and recycle greywater into potable water. The system was selected for UNICEF's Innovation30 programme in 2023 and was intended for use in homes, remote schools and healthcare facilities. UNICEF said Cycleau could cost less than US$500 per unit and recycle 20% of household greywater into potable water, while reducing the discharge of untreated wastewater.Turning used water into a resourceGreywater usually comes from domestic activities such as washing, bathing and laundry, rather than toilets. Although it is different from sewage, it can still contain microorganisms, chemicals and other contaminants, meaning it cannot be considered safe to collect and drink without treatment. Cycleau was designed to combine multiple water-treatment techniques within a single compact device. The system could be connected to existing water and drainage pipes serving a sink, bathroom or laundry area, allowing some of the greywater that would otherwise flow directly into the sewage system to be diverted for treatment and reuse.As Florea developed the concept, the technology became more refined. According to MIT Solve, the system was being designed as a modular, point-of-use treatment unit measuring roughly 24 by 36 inches. It was intended to capture greywater and treat it on site, while also addressing concerns about contaminants in household water supplies. The treatment train combined several methods rather than depending on a single filter. That layered approach reflects a basic principle of potable water reuse: different treatment processes are used to tackle different types of contaminants. Research published in Water Research examined decentralised greywater treatment using membrane bioreactors and moving-bed biofilm reactors followed by ultraviolet or electrochemical disinfection. The study found that combining biological treatment with disinfection could provide effective treatment while also highlighting the different strengths and limitations of each process.The promise and limits of decentralised treatmentThe appeal of a system such as Cycleau lies in bringing water treatment closer to where water is used. Rather than sending all household wastewater through a central network, a compact unit could divert and treat a portion of it for potential reuse. This approach could be useful in places where conventional water infrastructure is expensive to build or difficult to extend. UNICEF identified homes, remote schools and healthcare facilities as potential settings for Cycleau, particularly in communities facing water shortages or limited access to reliable water services.However, Cycleau was still an emerging technology in 2023, rather than a proven replacement for conventional drinking-water treatment. MIT Solve reported that the team was developing and testing automated prototypes and planned further evaluation of their ability to remove contaminants. Early testing also came with an important limitation: volunteers were instructed not to drink the water produced by the prototype. The technology therefore still required further testing and validation before it could be considered suitable for producing water for household consumption.From prototype to wider water reuseAccording to UNICEF, Cycleau had moved beyond the Innovation30 demonstration phase and entered a pilot project in collaboration with UNICEF in Tajikistan. In 2024, UNICEF stated that installing Cycleau in buildings could reduce their water footprint by up to 80%. This figure referred to the potential reduction in overall water use associated with the technology, rather than meaning that Cycleau could collect and reuse 80% of a building's greywater. Its underlying concept was to treat and recycle water that would otherwise have been discharged, potentially reducing the need for fresh water from conventional sources. However, the amount that could be recovered and reused would depend on the building, the installation and how the system was operated. For communities facing water shortages, the appeal was therefore not simply in treating wastewater, but in creating another opportunity to reuse water close to where it was originally consumed. Instead of relying entirely on additional supplies from reservoirs, rivers or aquifers, some of the demand could potentially be met by water already flowing through the building.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More than 1,000 volunteers built a four-bedroom house in just 50 hours; the unusual effort launched a 35-home community in San Antonio
articles.summary: US News: Building a four-bedroom home usually takes far longer than a single weekend, but more than 1,000 volunteers in San Antonio did it in just 50 hours. Th.
articles.body: Building a four-bedroom home usually takes far longer than a single weekend, but more than 1,000 volunteers in San Antonio did it in just 50 hours. The unusual project, organised by Habitat for Humanity of San Antonio & Guadalupe Valley, brought volunteers, interns, family and friends together to build a home for single mother Yadira Salas and her three children. Working in two-hour shifts, they raised walls, carried timber, installed windows and worked on the garden as the clock counted down. Salas also joined the construction effort, putting in her own “sweat equity” as the house took shape around her.How 1,000 volunteers helped build a four-bedroom homeThis was central to meeting the 50-hour deadline. Michael Taylor, president and CEO of Habitat for Humanity of San Antonio & Guadalupe Valley, told the San Antonio Express-News that more than 1,000 volunteers participated. Rather than having everyone work at once, volunteers partook in two-hour shifts, helping construct interior and exterior walls that would also be used for future Habitat houses.The first-hand report shows how many different groups contributed to the build. Alongside volunteers, six high-school and six college summer interns worked on the project, while volunteers carried and stacked lumber and helped raise framed walls. The result was a construction effort that depended on a group of people completing individual jobs in sequence rather than relying on one conventional building crew.Homeowner helped build her own four-bedroom houseAs reported by the San Antonio Express, Salas was not merely the recipient of the finished house. She spent long hours at the site working alongside the volunteers, putting in labour that Habitat describes as “sweat equity”. The San Antonio Express-News reported that she helped with the exterior wall siding, windows and lawn, allowing her to take an active role in creating the home where she and her children would live.For Salas, that involvement became one of the most meaningful parts of the project. “You feel grateful. You see your home and you're like, ‘Wow, we did this,’” she said in the report. Her route to homeownership had also taken several attempts: she applied to the Habitat programme twice before being accepted on her third application, with staff helping her complete the required paperwork.300-hour work commitment behind Habitat homesThe 50-hour build was an accelerated example of Habitat for Humanity’s broader approach to affordable homeownership. The organisation works with low-income families to build homes at no profit and zero interest. Families are expected to contribute more than 300 hours of work, including construction work on their own homes and on other families’ houses, as well as homebuyer-readiness classes.The wider development also had support beyond the volunteer workforce. Funding from the city of San Antonio and Bexar County covered streets, drainage and pavements for the new community, while Methodist Healthcare Ministries sponsored the 50-hour build. Alan Kramer, Methodist Healthcare’s chief financial officer, described housing as the foundation on which communities are built and thanked those who helped construct the home.Salas called the finished home a “big gift”The finished property was more than a one-off construction challenge. Salas’s house was the first of 35 planned homes in Methodist Meadows, meaning the 50-hour project also marked the beginning of a larger Habitat community. The San Antonio-area chapter had already dedicated its 1,500th Habitat home in April, while the organisation said more than 11,000 people volunteer their time each year.At the dedication ceremony, Salas welcomed those involved into her new home and called it “a big gift” for herself and her children. In the first-hand account, the 50-hour deadline therefore becomes only part of the story: the unusual construction schedule shows what a large, carefully organised volunteer effort could achieve, and the homeowner’s own labour made the project personal. “It’s a big accomplishment for myself as a single parent,” Salas said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ashington MP says government not helping Nepal manhunt
articles.summary: Ian Lavery says there has been a lack of help for a constituent missing in the Nepal floods.
articles.body:
An MP has accused the government of failing to help one of his constituents who has been missing since a deadly flood struck Nepal last month.

Ashington and Blyth MP Ian Lavery told parliament the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) has refused to directly assist in the hunt for Newbiggin-by-the-Sea resident Anirban Battacharyya who, despite living in the UK for 60 years, maintains Indian citizenship.

Lavery asked for urgent talks on how the government "can be more helpful to people who have lived in this country all their lives" but don't have citizenship.

The government said it was "in contact" with Indian authorities regarding "relief efforts".

More than 1,000 people are known to have died , and thousands remain missing, after a flash flood believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse swept through Nepalese border villages on 26 August.

Battacharyya was travelling between Kolkata in India and Nepal's capital Kathmandu when he was lost in the flooding and has not been heard from since, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

On Thursday, Lavery said: "The FCO have been less than helpful, pointing the family to the Indian Consulate who again have been less than helpful.

"Because he hasn't got a British passport, we can't help him?"

Responding for the government, the Leader of the Commons and Tynemouth MP Alan Campbell said he would see if the relevant minister will meet Lavery to discuss the case.

Campbell said: "We are working with authorities on the ground to support efforts in this terrible situation, supporting survivors of all nationalities and working to get families information about missing loved ones.

"We're also in contact with the Indian authorities about the relief efforts. I am disappointed that this hasn't led to the outcome that my honourable friend seeks."

articles.title: While surveying a California creek for threatened red-legged frogs, a scientist spotted what looked like a rock; it was an intact mastodon molar estimated to be 10,000 years old
articles.summary: US News: A routine field survey in a California redwood forest has led to an extraordinary glimpse into the Ice Age. A scientist searching a San Mateo County c.
articles.body: A routine field survey in a California redwood forest has led to an extraordinary glimpse into the Ice Age. A scientist searching a San Mateo County creek for signs of habitat conditions for threatened California red-legged frogs spotted an oddly shaped object that initially appeared to be an ordinary rock. Instead, it turned out to be a remarkably well-preserved tooth belonging to an extinct Pacific mastodon. The fossil is estimated to be at least 10,000 years old and is being described as an exceptionally complete specimen from the region.According to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen), geomorphologist Brigid Lynch discovered the fossil while working on a habitat enhancement project for California red-legged frogs. Paleontologists later confirmed that the object was an intact molar from an adult Pacific mastodon, a giant herbivore that once roamed parts of western North America.From a strange-looking rock to an Ice Age fossilLynch, who works with Balance Hydrologics, was surveying a creek bed when she noticed the unusual object. Its shape was distinctive enough to catch her attention, but there was initially no indication that it had survived from a prehistoric animal. Paleontologists later examined the object and identified it as a molar from a Pacific mastodon. The condition of the fossil made the discovery particularly significant. Wayne Thompson, a paleontologist and owner of Pacific Paleontology, described it as the most complete mastodon molar from the area and among the most impressive he had seen.The exact location of the discovery has not been disclosed. Midpen officials said the information was being kept private partly to prevent people from attempting to search the area themselves for fossils.A giant herbivore from California's pastThe fossil belonged to Mammut pacificus, commonly known as the Pacific mastodon. Although mastodons are often associated with the better-known American mastodon, scientists recognise the Pacific mastodon as a distinct species. The species was formally recognised in 2019 following research on mastodon remains from Southern California. Pacific mastodons differed from American mastodons in several physical characteristics, including narrower teeth, thicker leg bones and differences in their tusks.These animals were large herbivores that lived during the Pleistocene, an epoch that began roughly 2.5 million years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. They ranged across parts of western North America, with Pacific mastodon remains identified in California, Idaho, Oregon and, more recently, parts of Mexico. Unlike mammoths, which primarily grazed on grasses, mastodons were browsers that fed on leaves, shoots and other vegetation. That makes the newly discovered tooth more than just an unusual fossil. It is a physical remnant of a landscape that existed thousands of years before modern California took shape.What the tooth could revealThe fossil has now been donated to Stanford University's Doerr School of Sustainability for further study. Researchers plan to use carbon dating to determine its precise age rather than relying solely on the current estimate of at least 10,000 years. Scientists also intend to create a three-dimensional scan of the tooth. Midpen plans to use the resulting digital model and a replica for educational and public outreach purposes.According to the researchers, fossils such as this can help reconstruct past ecosystems and biodiversity. By studying what lived in a region thousands of years ago, scientists can gain a better understanding of how landscapes and species have changed over time. The discovery also creates an unexpected link between modern conservation and ancient history. Lynch was searching the landscape to support the habitat of a threatened frog species when she encountered evidence of an animal that disappeared thousands of years ago.For a moment, the creek bed offered a glimpse of a very different California, one where enormous mastodons moved through forests and other now-extinct animals shared the landscape. Today, that same environment is being studied and protected for species that are still here, making the accidental discovery a reminder of how dramatically ecosystems can change over time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A ‘beer party’ trap: Man kills friend with iron rod over suspected affair with wife
articles.summary: REWARI: Rewari Police have claimed to have cracked the murder of 40-year-old Jitender, whose body was found near the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation L.
articles.body: REWARI: Rewari Police have claimed to have cracked the murder of 40-year-old Jitender, whose body was found near the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) refinery on September 7.Police said Jitender was allegedly murdered by his friend, Praveen alias Papla, along with his nephew Aman Kumar, over suspicion that Jitender was having an illicit relationship with Praveen’s wife. Both accused have been arrested.According to police, the incident took place on the road leading towards Bhadawas village, near the HPCL refinery. The investigation was launched after police received information on September 7 that the body of a man was lying on the roadside.ASP Deepika Aggarwal, IPS, told reporters at a press conference on Friday that the Model Town police team rushed to the spot after receiving information about the body.A Scene of Crime team was also called to the location to conduct a detailed inspection and collect scientific evidence.Police said the deceased had sustained deep injuries to his head, apparently caused by a heavy object, and had suffered substantial blood loss.An iPhone was recovered from the pocket of the deceased’s trousers. He was subsequently identified as 40-year-old Jitender, a resident of Kamalpur village.Police took the body into custody and sent it to Civil Hospital, Rewari, for postmortem examination. After the postmortem, the body was handed over to the family.According to police, Jitender’s uncle Uttam Singh named his fellow villager Praveen alias Papla and another associate in his statement to police, expressing suspicion that they had attacked Jitender on the head and killed him.Following the complaint, a murder case was registered at Model Town police station in Rewari and an investigation was initiated.During the investigation, teams of CIA Rewari and Model Town police worked on technical evidence and confidential inputs. Police said their investigation eventually led to the arrest of Praveen alias Papla and Aman Kumar on Thursday.During interrogation, police said Praveen disclosed the alleged sequence of events leading to the murder.According to police, Praveen suspected that Jitender was involved in an illicit relationship with his wife. Driven by suspicion and resentment, he allegedly decided to eliminate Jitender.Police said that on the day of the incident, Praveen called Jitender to a liquor outlet in Kamalpur village on the pretext of having a beer party.The two subsequently went to a canal culvert, where they drank beer. Praveen then took Jitender along to pick up his nephew Aman Kumar from the Minda company.After picking up Aman, the three allegedly travelled in a car to a secluded road near the HPCL refinery leading towards Bhadawas village.According to the police account, Jitender got out of the vehicle to relieve himself. At that point, Praveen allegedly took advantage of the situation and attacked him from behind with a heavy iron rod kept inside the vehicle.Police said Aman allegedly kept watch on the road and monitored people approaching the area while the attack was carried out.After the alleged murder, the two accused reportedly fled the spot in the vehicle.Police said technical evidence and confidential information played a key role in tracing and arresting the two accused.The accused were produced before a court, which granted police three days’ remand.According to police, the remand will be used to recover the vehicle allegedly used in the crime, the iron rod and other evidence connected with the murder.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: Opposition manager calls Arsenal ‘the best team in Europe’
articles.summary: Sunderland manager Regis Le Bris has suggested Arsenal are the best team in Europe at the moment, ahead of his team’s game against the Gunners.Photo by Georg...
articles.body:
Sunderland manager Regis Le Bris has suggested Arsenal are the best team in Europe at the moment, ahead of his team's game against the Gunners.

Arsenal travel away to Sunderland to play at the Stadium of Light on Saturday night, with another opportunity to improve on dropped points from last season.

The Gunners have already turned last season's defeat away to Aston Villa into a win, and they now have the opportunity to better last season's 2-2 draw in the north east.

Arsenal comfortably walked to a 3-0 victory against Sunderland at home, but the Black Cats have been a different proposition at their own ground, and it's up to Saturday's away side to overcome that.

Photo by Justin Setterfield/Getty Images

For what it's worth, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris is expecting a very tough game, offering plenty of praise to Arsenal ahead of the match.

"It's still early in the season but they look so strong everywhere," Le Bris said . "The bench, every phase, they are just the best team in Europe I think at the minute.

"They have good momentum as well. It's a good challenge. We need these challenges to get better.

"I think we earned last year (in the Arsenal draw) the opportunity to go again and enjoy it."

Arsenal will hope to prevent Sunderland taking much enjoyment from the fixture, but they've certainly had the tougher preparation for the weekend fixture.

Whilst Sunderland played at home in the League Cup on Tuesday, Arsenal were away in the Champions League on Wednesday. The Gunners are in a run of four consecutive away games, with the Sunderland match followed by trips to Ipswich and then Brighton .

But Mikel Arteta won't want his team making any excuses. The Premier League is as competitive as ever, and the longer Arsenal can keep their five-game winning run going, the better their chances of sticking around in the title race.
